title: Greetings & Basics
pronunciation_focus_summary: Double consonants — Italian distinguishes between single and double consonants. Holding the consonant longer changes meaning entirely (e.g., pena vs penna). Found in buongiorno, piacere, grazie, and many everyday words.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'gn' cluster is not a palatal nasal here — 'buon' and 'giorno' are separate components. The 'gi' sounds like English 'j' in 'joy'. Stress falls on the 'or' syllable.
Stress on 'se'. The 'e' is open as in 'bed'. The 's' between vowels stays unvoiced in standard Italian.
Double 't' — hold the 't' sound slightly longer than in English. The 'o' in 'notte' is open. This is only used when saying goodbye at night or before bed, never as a greeting.
The 'ci' makes a 'ch' sound before 'ao'. This is one syllable — the 'a' and 'o' form a diphthong. Only use with friends, family, or people you address with 'tu'.
Double 'r' — trill it or at least tap it twice. The 'ci' at the end is 'chee'. Stress falls on 'der'. This is the standard polite goodbye.
The 'v' is like English 'v'. Stress on 'vo'. The final 'e' is always pronounced in Italian — never drop it.
The 'z' in 'grazie' is unvoiced, like 'ts' in 'cats'. Two syllables: GRAH-tsyeh. The 'ie' is a quick diphthong. Stress is on the first syllable.

phrases.translation: Thank you very much (lit. 'a thousand thanks')
phrases.pronunciation_notes: Double 'l' in 'mille' — hold the 'l' longer. The 'e' at the end is pronounced. 'Mille' means 'a thousand'.
The 'e' is open, like in 'bed'. The 'g' is hard as in 'go'. Two syllables with stress on the first. Also used to mean 'please, go ahead' or 'after you'.
The 's' in 'scusi' is unvoiced before 'c'. The 'u' is pure, like 'oo' in 'food'. The final 'i' is clear. Use this with strangers and in formal situations.
Similar to 'scusi' but informal. The 's' before 'c' is unvoiced. Use with friends or people your age in casual settings.
Simple and clean — just like 'see' in English. No accent mark (si with an accent means 'oneself' or 'if').
The 'o' is open, slightly shorter than the English 'no'. Keep it crisp.
Two short words. 'Come' has a closed 'o' and the final 'e' is always pronounced. 'Sta' is one clean syllable. Use with strangers, elders, and in formal settings.
Three words flowing together. 'Molto' — closed 'o', clear 'l'. 'Bene' — open 'e' like 'bed', final 'e' pronounced. Standard polite response to 'Come sta?'.

dialogues.context: Meeting someone at a formal event

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.translation: Very well, thank you. And you?

exchanges.speaker: other
exchanges.translation: Well, thank you. Nice to meet you!

dialogues.notes: Use 'Lei' (capitalized) for formal 'you'. It takes third-person verb forms. Always default to Lei with strangers.

dialogues.context: Asking for help on the street
dialogues.notes: 'Mi scusi' is the standard way to get a stranger's attention politely. 'Prego' as a response to thanks is universal in Italian.

dialogues.context: Running into a friend on the street
dialogues.notes: With friends, use 'tu' (informal you) and 'come stai?' instead of 'come sta?'. 'A presto' is a warm, casual goodbye meaning 'see you soon'.

cultural_notes.title: Formal vs Informal: Tu and Lei
cultural_notes.content: Italian has two forms of 'you': 'tu' (informal) and 'Lei' (formal). Use 'Lei' with strangers, older people, officials, and in professional settings. Use 'tu' with friends, family, children, and peers in casual situations. When in doubt, start with 'Lei' — the other person will often say 'Diamoci del tu!' (Let's use tu!) if they want to switch. Getting this wrong is not a disaster, but using 'tu' with an elder stranger can come across as disrespectful.

cultural_notes.title: Greetings involve physical contact
cultural_notes.content: Italians typically greet friends and acquaintances with two light kisses on the cheeks, starting from the left cheek. Between men, a firm handshake is more common unless they are close friends or family. In formal or business settings, a handshake is standard for everyone. Italians also tend to stand closer during conversation than Northern Europeans or Americans — this is normal and not an invasion of personal space.
